title: Block Cipher Modes — ECB, CBC, CTR, CFB

questions.question: In ECB mode, what happens to two identical plaintext blocks encrypted under the same key?
options: They produce identical ciphertext blocks
They produce unrelated ciphertext blocks because ECB uses an IV
They produce identical ciphertext only if the plaintext is ASCII
They produce identical ciphertext only if padding is disabled
questions.explanation: ECB encrypts each block independently: the same input block under the same key yields the same output block.

questions.question: In CTR mode, what must be true about nonce+counter values under a fixed key?
options: They must never repeat (keystream reuse breaks confidentiality)
They must be unpredictable, but repetition is fine
They must be secret, but repetition is fine
They must increase by exactly 1 across all devices globally
questions.explanation: CTR generates a keystream by encrypting nonce||counter; reusing the same nonce+counter under a key repeats the keystream and leaks relationships between plaintexts.

questions.question: PKCS#7 padding rule: if a message is already an exact multiple of the block size, what padding is added?
options: A full block of padding bytes, each equal to the block size
No padding bytes are added
A single 0x00 byte is added
Padding is random bytes of any length
questions.explanation: PKCS#7 always adds padding; when the length is already aligned, it adds an extra full block so unpadding is unambiguous.

questions.question: CBC decryption: which formula recovers plaintext block P_i (with C_0 = IV)?
options: P_i = D_K(C_i) ⊕ C_{i-1}
P_i = E_K(C_i) ⊕ C_{i-1}
P_i = D_K(C_{i-1}) ⊕ C_i
P_i = E_K(P_i) ⊕ C_{i-1}
questions.explanation: CBC decrypts each ciphertext block, then XORs with the previous ciphertext (or IV for the first block).

questions.question: Malleability intuition: in CTR mode, what is the effect of flipping one bit in the ciphertext?
options: The same bit flips in the decrypted plaintext at that position
The entire message decrypts to random garbage
Only the next block is corrupted, not the flipped position
Decryption fails with a padding error
questions.explanation: CTR is XOR with a keystream; flipping a ciphertext bit flips the corresponding plaintext bit unless an integrity check is added.

questions.question: Attack intuition: two CTR ciphertexts are produced with the same key and the same nonce/counter sequence. What can an attacker compute from the ciphertexts alone?
options: P1 ⊕ P2
P1 and P2 exactly
The secret key
The nonce (even if it was never transmitted)
questions.explanation: With keystream reuse, C1 = P1 ⊕ S and C2 = P2 ⊕ S, so C1 ⊕ C2 = P1 ⊕ P2.

questions.question: In CFB mode decryption, which block-cipher operation is used to generate the keystream?
options: Block-cipher encryption E_K(·) (not D_K)
Block-cipher decryption D_K(·) (not E_K)
Both E_K and D_K are required on every block
Neither; CFB never calls the block cipher once initialized
questions.explanation: CFB uses E_K on the feedback register (previous ciphertext/IV) to produce a keystream that is XORed with data.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about integrity for ECB/CBC/CTR/CFB?
options: None of them provide integrity by themselves; you need AEAD or a MAC
CBC provides integrity because it chains blocks
CTR provides integrity because counters prevent tampering
ECB provides integrity because blocks are independent
questions.explanation: These classic modes are confidentiality-only; they are malleable without an authentication tag (AEAD) or a separate MAC.
